title: Sigmoid Attention Makes KV Eviction Stick
hook: Learned cache-eviction gates train softly but must delete hard at inference. Swap softmax for sigmoid attention and that jump stops hurting — even though sigmoid is the worse LM.
key_points: Learned KV eviction has a soft-to-hard mismatch: training attenuates token contributions, but memory is only saved when entries are physically deleted.
The study runs a controlled 2x2x2 sweep over attention type, learned gating, and positional encoding on GPT-2-scale models trained on OpenWebText.
Sigmoid attention is worse as a dense language model than softmax — but that is not the operating point that matters here.
Sigmoid-gated models delete KV entries with negligible perplexity change relative to their own no-eviction reference.
Under a matched live-cache protocol, learned sigmoid gates beat the authors' H2O and KeyDiff implementations; softmax gates did not uniformly do so.
Takeaway: attention normalization decides whether a training-time soft gate transfers cleanly to hard deletion.
content_html: Long-context serving lives or dies on the KV cache, and one popular way to shrink it is to learn which entries to drop. That approach carries a quiet inconsistency: during training the gate is differentiable, so it can only turn a token's contribution down; at inference you save memory only by physically removing the entry. The authors ask whether the attention substrate itself affects how badly that soft-to-hard transition hurts.
extra_html:
A controlled sweep

They train GPT-2-scale transformers on OpenWebText in a 2x2x2 design over attention type (softmax or sigmoid), learned gating, and positional encoding. Sigmoid attention comes out worse as a dense language model — the expected result. But the useful operating point is different: sigmoid-gated models delete KV entries with negligible perplexity change relative to their own no-eviction reference, while softmax-gated ones degrade.

Against post-hoc baselines

Under a matched live-cache protocol on the same dense backbones, learned sigmoid gates achieved lower perplexity than the authors' implementations of H2O and KeyDiff, whereas softmax gates did not uniformly beat those post-hoc methods. The scale is small and the baselines are reimplementations, so treat the numbers as directional. The idea is the interesting part: normalization choices that look like a pure quality trade-off in dense training can determine whether a compression scheme works at all.

related.title: The KV Cache & Continuous Batching
related.hook: Generating one token reuses every prior key and value - that growing cache is why LLM inference is memory-bound, and continuous batching is how servers fight back.

related.title: ReFreeKV: Threshold-Free KV Cache Compression
related.hook: Most KV-cache pruning needs a hand-tuned budget threshold per input — pick wrong and performance craters. ReFreeKV adapts the budget on the fly instead.

related.title: Top-k KV Eviction Can't Know What It Threw Away
related.hook: Deterministic cache eviction is blind by construction: nothing you kept reveals how much error the deletions caused. Sample randomly instead and the leftovers become a statistical certificate.

flashcards.prompt: What is the soft-to-hard mismatch in learned KV-cache eviction?
flashcards.back_html: Training uses differentiable gates that merely attenuate a token's contribution, but inference only saves memory if the KV entry is actually removed — so the trained behaviour and the deployed behaviour differ.

flashcards.prompt: What is the counterintuitive finding about sigmoid attention here?

choices.text: It is worse as a dense language model, yet tolerates hard KV deletion far better
It matches softmax on perplexity and also evicts better
It removes the need for positional encodings entirely
It makes the KV cache unnecessary

flashcards.explanation_html: The paper separates the two operating points: dense quality favours softmax, but the transfer from soft gate to hard deletion favours sigmoid.

flashcards.prompt: What broader design lesson do the authors draw?
flashcards.back_html: Attention normalization is not neutral with respect to compression — the choice of substrate can decide whether a training-time gate survives being made hard at inference.
